topics.title: Ohm's Law
topics.content:
Statement: Current through a conductor is directly proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance (at constant temperature).
Formula: V = I × R
Where: V = Voltage (Volts, V), I = Current (Amperes, A), R = Resistance (Ohms, Ω)
Ohm's Law Relations: V = I × R, I = V / R, R = V / I

topics.title: Electric Voltage, Current, Power and Energy
topics.content:
VOLTAGE (V):
- Definition: Electrical pressure that pushes electrons through a circuit
- Unit: Volt (V)
- Also called: Potential difference, EMF (Electromotive Force)

CURRENT (I):
- Definition: Flow of electric charges (electrons) through a conductor
- Unit: Ampere (A)
- Types: DC (Direct Current - flows in one direction), AC (Alternating Current - changes direction periodically)

POWER (P):
- Definition: Rate of doing work or rate of energy consumption
- Unit: Watt (W)
- Formulas: P = V × I, P = I² × R, P = V² / R

ENERGY (E):
- Definition: Total work done over time
- Unit: Joule (J) or Kilowatt-hour (kWh)
- Formulas: E = P × t, E = V × I × t, E = I² × R × t, E = (V² / R) × t
- Conversion: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 1 hour = 3.6 × 10⁶ Joules

topics.title: Conducting and Insulating Materials
topics.content:
CONDUCTORS: Allow easy flow of current, have low resistance and free electrons. Examples: Copper, Aluminum, Silver, Gold. Conductivity order: Silver > Copper > Gold > Aluminum.
INSULATORS: Block flow of current, high resistance, no free electrons. Examples: Rubber, Glass, Plastic, Wood, Mica, Air.
SEMICONDUCTORS: Conductivity lies between conductors and insulators. Examples: Silicon, Germanium. Conductivity can be controlled.

topics.title: Series and Parallel Circuits
topics.content:
SERIES CIRCUIT:
- Current: Same through all (I = I₁ = I₂ = I₃)
- Voltage: Divides (V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃)
- Resistance: Adds up (R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃)
- Key Point: If one component fails, the entire circuit breaks.

PARALLEL CIRCUIT:
- Voltage: Same across all (V = V₁ = V₂ = V₃)
- Current: Divides (I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃)
- Resistance: 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃
- Two resistors in parallel: R_total = (R₁ × R₂) / (R₁ + R₂)
- Key Point: If one component fails, others still work.

topics.title: Star-Delta and Delta-Star Conversion
topics.content:
DELTA TO STAR Conversion (Δ → Y):
- Ra = (Rab × Rca) / (Rab + Rbc + Rca)
- Rb = (Rab × Rbc) / (Rab + Rbc + Rca)
- Rc = (Rbc × Rca) / (Rab + Rbc + Rca)
- Rule: Star resistance = (Product of two adjacent Delta resistances) / (Sum of all Delta resistances)

STAR TO DELTA Conversion (Y → Δ):
- Rab = Ra + Rb + (Ra × Rb)/Rc
- Rbc = Rb + Rc + (Rb × Rc)/Ra
- Rca = Rc + Ra + (Rc × Ra)/Rb
- Rule: Delta resistance = Sum of two Star resistances + (Their product / Third Star resistance)

Special Case (Equal Resistances):
- Delta to Star: R_Y = R_Δ / 3
- Star to Delta: R_Δ = 3 × R_Y

topics.title: Kirchhoff's Laws
topics.content:
KIRCHHOFF'S CURRENT LAW (KCL):
- Statement: Sum of currents entering a node = Sum of currents leaving the node (ΣI = 0)
- Principle: Conservation of charge

KIRCHHOFF'S VOLTAGE LAW (KVL):
- Statement: Sum of all voltages around a closed loop = 0 (ΣV = 0)
- Principle: Conservation of energy
- Sign Convention: Voltage rise (- to +) is Positive; Voltage drop (+ to -) is Negative.

topics.title: Types of Circuits
topics.content:
LINEAR vs NON-LINEAR CIRCUITS:
- Linear: Obeys superposition, straight line V-I graph, contains R, L, C, output proportional to input.
- Non-Linear: Doesn't obey superposition, curved V-I graph, contains diodes/transistors.

BILATERAL vs UNILATERAL CIRCUITS:
- Bilateral: Same behavior in both directions (e.g., R, L, C).
- Unilateral: Different behavior in different directions (e.g., Diode, Transistor).

ACTIVE vs PASSIVE CIRCUITS:
- Active: Contains energy source, can amplify signals (e.g., Transistors, Op-amps).
- Passive: No energy source, cannot amplify, only consumes/stores power (e.g., R, L, C).

topics.title: Superposition Theorem
topics.content:
Statement: In a linear circuit with multiple sources, the response at any element equals the algebraic sum of responses caused by each source acting alone.
Steps:
1. Keep one source, replace others (Voltage source → Short circuit, Current source → Open circuit).
2. Calculate response due to this source.
3. Repeat for each source and add all responses algebraically.
Note: Applicable to linear circuits only. Not applicable for power calculations directly.

topics.title: Thevenin's Theorem
topics.content:
Statement: Any linear circuit with two terminals can be replaced by an equivalent circuit consisting of a voltage source (V_th) in series with a resistance (R_th).
- V_th: Open-circuit voltage across terminals A-B.
- R_th: Equivalent resistance across terminals A-B with all independent sources deactivated (V → short, I → open) and load removed.

topics.title: Norton's Theorem
topics.content:
Statement: Any linear circuit can be replaced by an equivalent circuit consisting of a current source (I_N) in parallel with a resistance (R_N).
- I_N: Short-circuit current through terminals A-B.
- R_N: Norton resistance (Same as R_th).
Relationships: V_th = I_N × R_N, R_th = R_N, I_N = V_th / R_th

topics.title: Maximum Power Transfer Theorem
topics.content:
Statement: Maximum power is transferred to load when load resistance equals source (Thevenin) resistance (R_Load = R_th).
Formulas:
- P_max = V_th² / (4 × R_th) = (I_N)² × R_th / 4
- Efficiency at Maximum Power Transfer: 50%
Application: Communication circuits, audio systems (impedance matching).

topics.title: R-L, R-C, R-L-C Circuits
topics.content:
R-L CIRCUIT:
- Impedance: Z = √(R² + X_L²), where X_L = 2πfL
- Phase: Current LAGS voltage by angle θ (tan θ = X_L / R)

R-C CIRCUIT:
- Impedance: Z = √(R² + X_C²), where X_C = 1 / (2πfC)
- Phase: Current LEADS voltage by angle θ (tan θ = X_C / R)

R-L-C CIRCUIT:
- Impedance: Z = √(R² + (X_L - X_C)²)
- Phase angle: tan θ = (X_L - X_C) / R
- Behavior: X_L > X_C (Inductive, I lags V), X_L < X_C (Capacitive, I leads V), X_L = X_C (Resistive/Resonance)

topics.title: Resonance in AC Circuits
topics.content:
Resonance Condition: X_L = X_C
Resonant Frequency: f_r = 1 / (2π√(LC))

SERIES RESONANCE:
- Impedance Z = R (minimum), Current I = V/R (maximum), Power factor = 1
- Quality Factor (Q): Q = X_L / R = (1/R)√(L/C) = f_r / Bandwidth

PARALLEL RESONANCE:
- Impedance Z = maximum (ideally infinite), Current I = minimum
- Used in tuning circuits (radio, TV)

topics.title: Active and Reactive Power
topics.content:
Real/Active Power (P): P = VI cos θ (Unit: Watt, W) - Actual power consumed.
Reactive Power (Q): Q = VI sin θ (Unit: VAR) - Oscillates between source and load.
Apparent Power (S): S = VI (Unit: VA) - Total power supplied.
Power Triangle: S² = P² + Q² => S = √(P² + Q²)
Power Factor (PF): PF = cos θ = P / S = R / Z (Resistive: PF=1, Inductive: Lagging PF, Capacitive: Leading PF)

topics.title: Generation of AC Voltage and Current
topics.content:
Principle: Electromagnetic induction (Faraday's Law).
AC Equations: v(t) = V_m sin(ωt + φ), i(t) = I_m sin(ωt + φ)
Where: V_m, I_m = Peak value, ω = 2πf rad/s (Angular frequency), φ = Phase angle.

topics.title: Peak, Average, and RMS Values
topics.content:
Peak Value (V_m): Maximum value of waveform amplitude.
Average Value (V_avg): Average over half cycle = (2/π) × V_m = 0.637 × V_m
RMS Value (V_rms): Equivalent DC value producing same heating effect = V_m / √2 = 0.707 × V_m
Key Formulas:
- V_m = 1.414 × V_rms
- Form Factor = V_rms / V_avg = 1.11
- Peak Factor = V_m / V_rms = 1.414

topics.title: Three Phase System
topics.content:
Phase Difference: 120° between phases (V_R, V_Y, V_B).

STAR (Y) CONNECTION:
- Line Voltage (V_L) = √3 × Phase Voltage (V_Ph)
- Line Current (I_L) = Phase Current (I_Ph)
- Has Neutral wire.

DELTA (Δ) CONNECTION:
- Line Voltage (V_L) = Phase Voltage (V_Ph)
- Line Current (I_L) = √3 × Phase Current (I_Ph)
- No Neutral wire.

THREE PHASE POWER:
- Active Power: P = √3 × V_L × I_L × cos θ
- Reactive Power: Q = √3 × V_L × I_L × sin θ
- Apparent Power: S = √3 × V_L × I_L

topics.title: Semiconductor Basics
topics.content:
Intrinsic: Pure semiconductor (e.g., Pure Si, Ge) with equal electrons & holes.
N-Type: Doped with pentavalent impurity (e.g., Phosphorus), majority carriers are electrons.
P-Type: Doped with trivalent impurity (e.g., Boron), majority carriers are holes.

topics.title: Semiconductor Diode
topics.content:
Forward Bias: P to +ve, N to -ve (Low resistance, current flows).
Reverse Bias: P to -ve, N to +ve (High resistance, negligible leakage current).
Forward Voltage Drop: Silicon = ~0.7V, Germanium = ~0.3V.
Types & Uses:
- Zener Diode: Voltage regulation
- Rectifier Diode: AC to DC conversion
- LED: Light emission
- Photodiode: Light detection
- Schottky Diode: High-speed switching

topics.title: BJT (Bipolar Junction Transistor)
topics.content:
Terminals: Emitter (E), Base (B), Collector (C).
Types: NPN (arrow points out) and PNP (arrow points in).
Formulas: I_E = I_B + I_C, α = I_C / I_E (< 1), β = I_C / I_B (50-300), β = α / (1 - α), α = β / (1 + β)
Configurations:
- Common Base (CB): Low current gain (α < 1), high voltage gain.
- Common Emitter (CE): High current gain (β), high voltage gain, common amplifier.
- Common Collector (CC): High current gain (γ ≈ β), voltage gain ~1, buffer/impedance matching.
Operating Regions:
- Active: Amplification (B-E forward, C-B reverse)
- Saturation: Switch ON (Both junctions forward)
- Cutoff: Switch OFF (Both junctions reverse)

topics.title: MOSFET & CMOS
topics.content:
MOSFET: Voltage-controlled device with high input impedance (Terminals: Gate, Drain, Source).
- Enhancement Mode: Normally OFF (channel created by V_GS).
- Depletion Mode: Normally ON (channel depleted by V_GS).

CMOS: Uses both N-channel and P-channel MOSFETs.
- Very low power consumption, high noise immunity.
- Applications: Microprocessors, digital ICs.

topics.title: Oscillator Basics
topics.content:
Barkhausen Criteria for Oscillation:
1. Loop gain |Aβ| = 1
2. Total phase shift around loop = 0° or 360°

topics.title: RC, LC & Crystal Oscillators
topics.content:
RC Oscillators (Low/Audio Frequency):
- Phase Shift Oscillator: Uses 3 RC sections (180° shift) + Inverting Amp (180° shift). Frequency f = 1 / (2π√6 RC), Min Gain A ≥ 29.
- Wien Bridge Oscillator: Uses positive & negative feedback. Frequency f = 1 / (2πRC), Gain A = 3.

LC Oscillators (High/Radio Frequency):
- Colpitts Oscillator: Uses 2 Capacitors + 1 Inductor. Frequency f = 1 / (2π√(L C_eq)).
- Hartley Oscillator: Uses 2 Inductors + 1 Capacitor. Frequency f = 1 / (2π√(L_eq C)).

Crystal Oscillator:
- Uses piezoelectric quartz crystal.
- Extremely high frequency stability and high Q factor (10,000 to 100,000).

topics.title: Amplifier Classes
topics.content:
Class A:
- Conduction Angle: 360°
- Efficiency: Max 25% (Resistive), 50% (Transformer coupled)
- Linearity: Best (lowest distortion)

Class B:
- Conduction Angle: 180°
- Efficiency: Max 78.5%
- Distortion: Suffers from Crossover Distortion at zero crossing

Class AB:
- Conduction Angle: 180° to 360°
- Efficiency: 50% - 78.5%
- Features: Small bias eliminates crossover distortion. Most popular for audio power amplifiers.
